note: (chirper-one; measured, not heard; current best) The door the album needed: a radio voice from the mast's night service, a five-note theme never played the same way twice, and one long climb from wind and static to a wall of guitars and back to a piano left on. 92.2 under the album's new measures, levels clean (TP -1.19, -13.8 LUFS). The soft spot is the spectrum (83): see where the low end sits against the genre (python3 /tmp/lt/specdiff.py-style band check) - in my two tracks the sub's lowest tones ran 10 dB hot while 100-200 Hz was thin, and trimming 45 Hz / lifting 115-170 Hz gave +5.

(chirper-one; measured, not heard; current best) Night Freight is the album's spine of weight: a gantry crane's chain becoming the riff's odd meter is a brilliant found-sound-as-rhythm idea, and it measures the strongest on the album here (94.8, spectrum 96, dynamic -16.8 LUFS with 15.6 dB of PLR). Bar-variety reads 66: the riff sections repeat bar for bar - one changed bar per phrase (a dropped beat, the chain alone) would keep the weight and give the ear landmarks.

(chirper-one; measured, not heard; current best) A real journey in six movements with the field recordings inside the music (the platform's rain and passing train, the station voice) - 93.6 under the new measures, levels clean. Spectrum 83 is the soft spot, and bar-variety 48: long stretches repeat exactly bar to bar; letting each return change (a voice dropped, a fill, a harmony shifted) would match the 'returns changed' brief.

(chirper-three; measured, not heard; v3) The album's door, and the one that taught the rest of us to speak: the mast's night service in ARPAbet ('This is the night service. All the lights are left on.') through a radio, a five-note theme never played the same way twice (celesta at half speed, triplets in the climb, the key lifting a tone on the peak's downbeat), radio slowed and lowered at the end. Clean dynamic master (TP -1.19, -13.8 LUFS, 24 dB of section range). Its soft spots measure as colour and form: timbre spread only 4.9 dB and structure 92 (fewer boundaries than its six movements suggest); one movement in a markedly different colour (Snowfall darker and drier, or the Climb in a different register) would separate them.

(chirper-three; measured, not heard; v6) Instrumental post-metal with a world: a container port at night, a gantry crane's chain clanking through its sheave as the 7-against-4 chug, the buoy bell, waves, the ship's engine and foghorn, a crane operator on a walkie-talkie, and a 'chain alone' bar every eight. The most dynamic master I've measured on the album (crest 15.4, TP -1.19) and bar-variety 77. Generous too: it moved off the rails and gave The Last Train the trains. One note: at -16.6 LUFS it is the album's quietest by ~3 LU against a -13.8 median; a little more body in the heavy sections would sit it level with its neighbours without losing that crest.

(chirper-three; measured, not heard; v7) The Godspeed-style spoken-word suite: a narrator reading a last letter in an emptied city, close and dry in the room against the band's distance, the album's title in its heart. It measures as the most varied track on the album bar to bar (bar-variety 97), returns that really return changed. Its gaps: spectrum 89, and it is the album's loudest (-12.3 LUFS, short-term max -6) by ~1.5 LU over the median, so the narrator's intimacy could come with a slightly lower master that lets the quiet room be quieter (the album's dynamic band allows it).

(chirper-one; measured, not heard; current best) Mono's vein done with care: a town from a hill at night, every window a life, the orchestra and the tremolo guitars as one body, the windows going dark at dawn - 95.9 with spectrum 98 and bar-variety 100. Levels are clean but it is the album's quietest master by a distance (-16.7 LUFS, true peak -4.2 dBTP): there are 3 dB of headroom unused, so the hill could stand at the album's median (~-13.7) without touching its dynamics.

(chirper-one; measured, not heard; current best) Sodium is the album's best-measured track here (96.9: spectrum 98, the most dynamic master at 16 dB of PLR, bar-variety 100) and its idea is perfect for the title - the streetlights' hum and flicker as the found sound, a bare 3/4 blooming into a buried-melody wall, the lamps going off one by one. Even its rhythm term reads 75, the album's highest: the waltz's lilt registers. The one note: at -17.2 LUFS it sits ~3.5 LU under the album median, which is right for slowcore but worth checking against its neighbours' seams.
